title: Vayera: here am I (Genesis 22:1, 7, 11)
hook: Abraham answers "here am I" to God, to his son and to the angel
tomorrow: Chayei Sarah: the life of Sarah

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaac was born, and Sarah's laugh turned from doubt to joy. Your line was laugh with me. Who did you laugh with? Today, the last day of Vayera, and its hardest chapter. Day one hundred eighty.

Someone calls your name from the next room. You say: yeah? What? In a minute. Half your mind is still on what you were doing. Now think of the few times you answered a call with all of you. A child crying at night, and you're up before you're awake. A friend on the phone, and you can hear that something's wrong, so you put everything down. There's a word in Hebrew for answering like that. It's not just yes. It means: I'm here, fully. Abraham says it three times in one chapter. Today's word.
screen: `YEAH? WHAT? IN A MINUTE.` → `ANSWERING WITH ALL OF YOU.` → `ONE WORD, THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: The word is hineni. Here I am. The chapter is Genesis twenty-two, which Jews call the Akedah, the binding of Isaac. It's one of the hardest stories in the Torah, and Jews have wrestled with it for centuries. It begins: "God did prove Abraham, and said unto him: 'Abraham'; and he said: 'Here am I.'" Then God tells him to take his son, his only son, whom he loves, Isaac, and offer him up on a mountain. Abraham rises early and goes. On the third day, father and son walk up the mountain together, Isaac carrying the wood. And Isaac speaks: "My father." And Abraham says: "Here am I, my son." The same word. Isaac asks where the lamb is, and Abraham says God will provide. Then, at the top, when Abraham has bound Isaac and raised the knife, an angel calls from heaven: Abraham, Abraham. And a third time he answers: here am I. And the angel says: don't lay your hand on the boy. Abraham sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it instead. Isaac is not harmed. Readers disagree deeply about this story. Many see Abraham's complete faith. Others read it as the Torah's way of rejecting child sacrifice, which other peoples of the time practiced. Some midrashim wonder whether Abraham should have argued, as he did for Sodom. All of them notice the word. Hineni, to God. Hineni, to his son. Hineni, to the angel who stops him. Fully present to each. Later, when God calls, the prophet Isaiah will answer: "Here am I; send me." So that's Vayera: a visit to the sick, an argument for justice, a stranger's goodness, a laugh of joy, and here am I.
screen: `GOD CALLS: HERE AM I.` · `ISAAC CALLS: HERE AM I, MY SON.` · `THE ANGEL CALLS: HERE AM I.` · `READERS DISAGREE DEEPLY.` · then, large: `HERE I AM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say here I am, and mean it. Settle, and breathe. Silently say: here I am. Notice where you actually are: your body, this room, this moment. Then think of someone who might call your name today, a child, a parent, a friend, a coworker. Picture answering them not with in a minute, but with all of you: here I am. If you pray, you can say it to God too. The bell holds the time.
Hineni. Here I am: not just yes, but fully present, Abraham's answer to God, to his son, and to the angel.
Your line: here I am. Today, when someone calls your name, put down what you're holding, turn, and answer with all of you. Day one hundred eighty.

howItsDone: The binding of Isaac, the Akedah, is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and many Jews recite it in the daily morning prayers; hineni is also the name of a prayer the cantor says before the Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur services in many communities.

fork.setup: you're Abraham, walking up the mountain with Isaac. he says, "My father." how do you answer?
fork.reveal: "Here am I, my son." the same word he said to God, now to his son. fully present to each.

original.note: Hebrew: here I am; fully present, ready.

trapdoor: what you thought: here I am just means I'm in the room.
what it means: hineni is answering with all of you, and Abraham says it to God, to his son and to the angel.
what a scholar hears: hineni at 22:1, 7, 11; Rashi on 22:1, 'a word of humility and readiness'; the Akedah read on Rosh Hashanah; Isaiah 6:8.

sources.quoted: God did prove Abraham, and said unto him: 'Abraham'; and he said: 'Here am I.'

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording and punctuation of Genesis 22:1, 22:7 ('My father.' / 'Here am I, my son.') and Isaiah 6:8.

Readings of the Akedah given side by side without ranking: supreme faith; rejection of child sacrifice (a common modern reading); midrashic wondering whether Abraham should have argued. Confirm fairness and whether a specific midrash should be cited for the third.
'Which other peoples of the time practiced' (child sacrifice in the ancient Near East): stated briefly; confirm the phrasing is careful enough.
The Akedah in the daily morning service and on the second day of Rosh Hashanah; the cantor's Hineni prayer (Ashkenazi High Holiday rite): confirm.
